**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on compute capacity for the next two quarters

We've been asked whether we should purchase additional local AI hardware or focus on improving utilisation of the fleet we already own. After several weeks of measurement, modelling, and argument, we have a recommendation, though it comes with honest caveats.

**Where we stand**

Our current utilisation sits at roughly 40 percent during business hours and drops below 15 percent overnight and on weekends. That headline number is misleading in both directions. The low average conceals genuine contention: our fine-tuning jobs and the inference serving behind the internal product compete for the same eight GPUs, and when they collide, queue times spike and the's p95 latency degrades from a comfortable 400 milliseconds to well over two seconds. So we are simultaneously underutilised in aggregate and capacity-constrained at peak. The problem is not that we lack hardware; it is that our hardware is scheduled badly.

**The case for buying**

Buying more GPUs would make the contention problem disappear by brute force. It would also add a real reliability margin: right now a single node failure removes a quarter of our capacity, and our redundancy story is thin. If the product grows as the roadmap suggests, demand will eventually exceed even a perfectly scheduled fleet. There is something to be said for not spending engineering time on scheduler plumbing when a purchase solves the problem outright.

But the economics are poor at our current utilisation. A meaningful expansion would cost on the order of $180,000 in capital plus power, cooling, and maintenance overhead, and it would be spent to serve demand we cannot yet demonstrate. Hardware also depreciates quickly in this market; a GPU bought today at peak pricing may be worth half that in eighteen months. And the purchase is only partially reversible — reselling used accelerators recovers some value, but not enough, and the floor space, power provisioning, and operational burden are stickier than the purchase order suggests.

**The case for improving utilisation**

The alternative is to treat our scheduling as an engineering problem, which it is. Three changes account for most of the opportunity. First, moving our batch fine-tuning runs to overnight and weekend windows, when the fleet is idle, would remove the largest source of peak contention at essentially zero cost. Second, adopting a proper queueing layer with priority classes — rather than the ad hoc first-come allocation we use now — would let us protect the's latency SLO while still filling the gaps with batch work. Third, right-sizing model deployments and enabling dynamic batching on the inference side should recover another 10 to 15 percent of effective capacity. Taken together, we believe these changes can push sustained utilisation above 70 percent and eliminate the peak-hour collisions that cause our worst-visible failures.

The opportunity cost of this path is real: it is perhaps six weeks of an engineer's time that could go toward product work, and scheduler work is unglamorous. But it is reversible in a way capital expenditure is not. If we build the scheduling layer and discover demand has outgrown it, we will have lost six weeks and gained infrastructure we would have needed anyway. If we buy hardware and demand disappoints, we are carrying sunk cost with no compensating benefit.

**Recommendation**

Improve utilisation first. Commit to the scheduling and batching work over the next quarter, with a concrete success criterion: sustained utilisation above 65 percent and p95 latency under 600 milliseconds at projected peak load. Revisit the purchase decision at the end of that quarter with real data in hand. If demand growth continues on its current trajectory, we will likely need new hardware by mid-next year regardless — but we should buy it because demand requires it, not because our scheduling is lazy. Buying time through better utilisation also lets us purchase later, when prices and the next hardware generation may both be more favourable.

**Uncertainty**

We want to be candid about what we don't know. Our demand forecast is extrapolated from three months of usage and could be wrong in either direction; a large internal customer adopting the would change the calculus immediately. Our utilisation targets are estimates, not measurements — some contention may prove structural rather than schedulable. And there is a scenario, which we take seriously, in which the engineering effort to improve utilisation runs over and delivers less than projected, leaving us worse off than if we had simply bought capacity in the first place. We have tried to size that risk, and we believe the asymmetry still favours the utilisation path: the downside is bounded and the work has value even if the purchase eventually happens.

We propose reconvening in eight weeks with measured results.
